why.why: Chronic bilateral glaucoma remains the leading hypothesis because the 10-year progressive bilateral visual field constriction with severe central vision loss and no afferent pupillary defect is most consistent with glaucoma. The radiologist’s analysis explicitly maintains glaucoma as the leading diagnosis; however, FAF hyperfluorescent foci raise the possibility of retinal dystrophy, and core diagnostic data—visual field pattern, cup-to-disc ratio, intraocular pressure, and OCT retinal nerve fiber layer thickness—are still missing. Confidence therefore remains moderate at 0.45.

The radiologist’s finding of FAF hyperfluorescent foci is an additional retinal sign that supports retinal dystrophy and cannot be excluded. This, combined with slowly progressive bilateral field constriction and no afferent pupillary defect, increases confidence in retinal dystrophy. However, glaucoma remains the leading hypothesis and confirmatory electroretinography/genetic testing is absent, so confidence is only moderately increased to 0.35.

The new FAF finding of hyperfluorescent foci points to retinal pathology rather than primary optic nerve disease, making bilateral optic neuropathy less likely. No optic nerve-specific testing was obtained, and the radiologist’s analysis does not support this diagnosis; confidence is reduced to 0.10.

Compressive chiasmal lesion remains unlikely because severe generalized field constriction without bitemporal hemianopia is atypical for chiasmal syndromes. The radiologist's focus on glaucoma and retinal dystrophy does not change this, and the existing evidence actively refutes the hypothesis; confidence is reduced to 0.05.
